questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go on exchange for many reasons. The main one would have to be the opportunity to better my academic English, more precisely legal English. I ultimately wanted to study abroad in an English speaking country which is why I chose England. Furthermore, I have been to London multiple times prior to my stay and have a lot of family that reside in London, it just seemed like the optimal place for me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: You get A LOT of e-mails prior to arriving in London with tons of details about the whole process. They cover most of the details, however there were a few times I had to reach out to their administration, especially when it came to my course registration.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They have a whole Global Opportunities team that is available for any inquiries. The first week at QMUL was an orientation week, where the Global Opportunities team provided a lot of information about the exchange stay and opportunities to meet other exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: My initial though and ambition was to find housing close to campus. I must however admit that I was out too late and the prices were significantly more expensive than I though. I therefore chose to stay with family that lived quite a bit far from campus, but it worked out fine. My recommendation to anyone looking for housing is to research very early on, I would even say in March. If you are looking to stay in student accommodation halls, the earlier the better. You can book these student accommodation rooms/studios from Denmark whereby you wont need to physically be in London. These sell out very quickly and can get very expensive. If you choose to stay in a privately rented room/apartment I would definently recommend you to see the housing first before paying anything to the landlord. There are unfortunantly a lot of scams going around, so be very careful. There is a lot of information regarding finding off campus housing on QMUL website, so I would definently recommend checking that out.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: First thing, it can get very expensive. There is a lot of people in this city and a huge demand on housing and a cost of living crisis going on right now. Keep this in mind, and make sure to start early to minimise the cost as much as possible. Also, getting a few people together to find a joint place is also a great way to do this. Secondly, London is a very big city so there are a lot of places to stay. My housing was an hour commute from campus, which could get a little annoying. I stayed in a nice area however so I was very satisfied. The area around QMUL is not the nicest, keep this in mind. Lastly, living off campus is a good opportunity to see other areas of London and really live like a local, so in that sense it was very nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: QMUL does not offer housing to european exchange students which is very unfortunate.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had to reach out to the administration a few times regarding this. They do answer fairly quickly however, and clear up any questions I had.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You will get some e-mails regarding course registration, but keep in mind that Law exchange students follow a separate course registration process. The way it happened to me was I received an e-mail of the available courses for me to choose from (around 12 different courses), where I had to fill out a google form of my priorities and they would grant you them based on how they would fit into your timetable.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could e-mail the administration, Global Opportunities team and Law faculty staff regarding any questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all my 4 first priorities. The first month or so there is an add/drop period where you have the chance to drop or add courses. I did not utilise this, but from what I heard from others, it was difficult to do. You can also request to change to a different team within your course if you want to take a class at a different time, which I did a few times successfully. You have to give good reason to have your request granted, which for me was that I lived an hour away from campus. This was very helpful, whereby I only had classes 2-3 times a week.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patient and ask all the questions. Not everything is in the available information so keep in mind that you may have to reach out to administration yourself.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had four courses, all worth 15 credits each (7.5 ECTS). I had 2 first year courses and 2 third year courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching varied from course to course. My first year courses had a mix of online and physical lectures and 1hour seminars/tutorials, while my third year courses were only 1 2hour seminar a week. Teaching comprised approximately 8 hours per week, and therefore less than at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Contract Law I: Formation and Vitiation, Law in Context, Cultural Diversity and the Law, Equality and the Law. The first 2 are first year courses, and the latter are third year courses.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend the course Contract Law I, that gives you a great insight to the principles of English contract law. Equality and the Law was also very enjoyable because it focused a lot on conducting research which was nice difference to what I had been used to at UCPH.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I do not recall any unexpected costs

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: London is very expensive. Transportation, eating out and social things are getting increasingly expensive so bear this in mind. I did not have to pay for books because I borrowed from the library. The library has every book you need for your courses and you can borrow them up to 52 weeks (given that no one else reserves them).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of clubs and sportsteams you can join on campus. I attended events for some of them and would recommend!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of cultural clubs for a lot of various nationalities. There were a lot of sportsteams for pretty much every sport you can think of. There were also a lot of social activities on campus, including fresher events. Fresher events are primarily for first year students, so the age group of most of the students attending is 17/18.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Attend all the things you can, most people had wonderful experiences.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See the city! London is huge and full of different people so you can never really be bored. There is a lot to do. Furthermore, take the opportunity to experience other cities in the UK. I visited Brighton and Edinburgh while I was there.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I have been to London a lot of times before and it is very similar to Copenhagen.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open. People are all on the same boat and eager to find friends. Don't be afraid to reach out to people, they are super nice.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not so much a cultural difference but there is a lot of people in London which can be very overwhelming.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: London is truly a melting pot of cultures. There is people from all walks of life from all over the world which is nice to live among.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Make sure to save up a lot in advance. Due to Brexit, the erasmus scholarship is no longer available for exchange students going to the UK. London is expensive, so you are better off saving up as much money in advance. 2) Research housing thoroughly and 3) Be open to get to know people

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I have covered everything above.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know people and making friends from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Everything is very overwhelming in the beginning, so taking time to adjust to all the changes was a bit challenging.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
